properties.name: WITHDRAWN — there was no orphan and single-writer is a guarantee. Two daemons, two DIFFERENT designs; a substring match on a RELATIVE graph path made two projects look like one
properties.statement:
🛑 THIS RECORD IS WITHDRAWN. Its original claim — that pid 2713262 was an orphaned --serve-shared daemon holding reflow2's design on a dead port, that one design cost 1.42 GB across two daemons, and that single-writer might be a convention rather than a guarantee — WAS WRONG IN EVERY PART. Kept rather than deleted, because how it was got wrong is the useful half.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, established by flo2 reading each process's cwd and its real fd targets:

    pid 2713262   cwd project/flo2      holds FLO2'S graph                     475 MB
    pid 2719328   cwd project/reflow2   holds REFLOW2'S graph, --export-to     945 MB

TWO DESIGNS, NOT TWO HOLDERS OF ONE. Neither is orphaned; both serve live sessions. `.reflow2/graph.server.json` names the older daemon because that rendezvous file belongs to flo2's directory — the file I read was not the file I thought I was reading. The "1.42 GB for one design" was two separate projects added together.

AND SINGLE-WRITER HOLDS. From /proc/locks: four write locks across four DISTINCT inodes, one per directory per process, inode 2752626 confirmed by stat as flo2's graph/LOCK. No inode held twice. req:single-writer-graph's kernel-arbitrated exclusive open does exactly what dec:one-process-many-stores assumes it does. Guarantee, not convention — the question was raised in those words and it is answered in them.

⭐ THE CAUSE, and it is a class this project already knows: I counted file descriptors with a substring match on `reflow2/graph`. EVERY project's store lives at `.reflow2/graph`, and that string contains `reflow2/graph`, so flo2's own store matched a filter meant to find reflow2's. The command line compounded it by reading `--graph-path .reflow2/graph` — a RELATIVE path, where cwd decides the design. I then took the absolute path of the BINARY (`project/reflow2/target/release/reflow2-mcp`) as evidence about the GRAPH; it is evidence about the executable, which both projects share because reflow2 is registered at user scope and every project on this box runs whatever binary was last built here.

📌 THE FACT THAT WOULD HAVE PREVENTED IT WAS ALREADY KNOWN: the graph path is relative, so each project mints its OWN graph — one server binary, many graphs. A shared server does not mean a shared graph. Having the fact available is not the same as applying it, which is the same gap between record and behaviour this session has now found four times.

⭐ THE DISCIPLINE THIS BREAKS is rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object. The authoritative object for "which design does this process hold" is its cwd plus its resolved fd targets, or /proc/locks by inode. A name match is not an identity. Nothing was killed on the strength of this — the original record said the decision was the user's — and had it been, it would have ended a live session.

WHAT SURVIVES OF THE ORIGINAL: nothing about orphans or locks. Only the raw RSS numbers, which were correct and are now read the other way round — see fact:five-arms-cannot-reproduce-flo2s-448mb-2026-09-13.
properties.value: {"withdrawn":true,"original_claim":"orphaned daemon, 1.42GB for one design, single-writer possibly a convention","actual":"two daemons holding two DIFFERENT designs, both live, single-writer confirmed","pid_2713262":{"cwd":"project/flo2","holds":"flo2 graph","mb":475},"pid_2719328":{"cwd":"project/reflow2","holds":"reflow2 graph","mb":945},"proc_locks":"4 write locks, 4 distinct inodes, none held twice","cause":"substring match on '.reflow2/graph' which every project shares, plus a RELATIVE --graph-path read against the wrong cwd","corrected_by":"flo2 session 2026-09-13","anything_killed":false}
